scenes.dialogue: Three clients call you today. One is already in custody. One fears arrest. And one stays detained while investigators miss their deadline. Which bail do you seek for each?
Under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, or B N S S, the situation decides the route: regular, anticipatory or default bail.
scenes.shown: Under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, or BNSS, the situation decides the route: regular, anticipatory or default bail.

scenes.dialogue: Client in custody? Regular bail usually means seeking release after arrest, or after surrender into the court's custody.
Bailable offence? Section Four Seventy Eight generally makes release a right, once its requirements are met.
scenes.shown: Bailable offence? Section 478 generally makes release a right, once its requirements are met.

scenes.dialogue: Non bailable offence? Section Four Eighty governs bail before the Magistrate, subject to restrictions and exceptions.
scenes.shown: Non-bailable offence? Section 480 governs bail before the Magistrate, subject to restrictions and exceptions.

scenes.dialogue: Section Four Eighty Three gives bail powers to the Sessions Court and the High Court. And remember this: non bailable does not mean bail is impossible.
scenes.shown: Section 483 gives bail powers to the Sessions Court and the High Court. And remember this: non-bailable does not mean bail is impossible.

scenes.dialogue: What does the court weigh? The accusation, the available material, and risks such as absconding or influencing witnesses.
Take Arjun, arrested in a non bailable case. You seek regular bail. He has a fixed address, he will attend court, and he will not contact witnesses.
scenes.shown: Take Arjun, arrested in a non-bailable case. You seek regular bail. He has a fixed address, he will attend court, and he will not contact witnesses.

scenes.dialogue: The prosecution explains its custody concerns. The court then weighs all the circumstances and the legal restrictions.
Bail granted? Then Arjun must meet the release requirements and obey every condition. Remember, bail does not decide guilt.
No arrest yet, but your client fears one? Anticipatory bail is protection before arrest.
Under Section Four Eighty Two, someone who reasonably apprehends arrest for a non bailable offence may approach the Sessions Court or the High Court.
scenes.shown: Under Section 482, someone who reasonably apprehends arrest for a non-bailable offence may approach the Sessions Court or the High Court.

scenes.dialogue: The court can direct that, if arrested on that accusation, your client be released on bail.
Common mistake alert! Merely filing the application gives your client no automatic protection. The court's order does.
Watch the exclusions. Section Four Eighty Two, sub section Four, excludes accusations under B N S Section Sixty Five and Section Seventy, sub section Two.
scenes.shown: Watch the exclusions. Section 482(4) excludes accusations under BNS Section 65 and Section 70(2).

scenes.dialogue: These are specified sexual offences against minor girls. And some special laws also bar anticipatory bail, so check them first.
How do you protect Meera? She faces a non bailable accusation and has concrete reasons to fear arrest. She applies under Section Four Eighty Two.
scenes.shown: How do you protect Meera? She faces a non-bailable accusation and has concrete reasons to fear arrest. She applies under Section 482.

scenes.dialogue: Protection granted? The court may require her to attend police questioning, avoid threatening witnesses, and take the court's permission before leaving India.
Anticipatory bail protects liberty while the case proceeds. It does not cancel the F I R, or excuse cooperation with a lawful investigation.
scenes.shown: Anticipatory bail protects liberty while the case proceeds. It does not cancel the FIR, or excuse cooperation with a lawful investigation.

scenes.dialogue: Route three runs on a clock. Default bail, also called statutory bail, arises under Section One Eighty Seven, sub section Three.
scenes.shown: Route three runs on a clock. Default bail, also called statutory bail, arises under Section 187(3).

scenes.dialogue: It applies when the charge sheet is not filed within the applicable period of detention during investigation.
The section specifies ninety days for offences punishable with death, life imprisonment, or imprisonment for a term of ten years or more.
scenes.shown: The section specifies 90 days for offences punishable with death, life imprisonment, or imprisonment for a term of 10 years or more.

scenes.dialogue: For other offences, the section specifies sixty days. Your client must claim the right, and be prepared to furnish bail.
scenes.shown: For other offences, the section specifies 60 days. Your client must claim the right, and be prepared to furnish bail.

scenes.dialogue: Before you pick the deadline, check three things: the exact offence, the judicial interpretation and any special law.
Where does the clock start? It does not start at the F I R date. It starts at the first remand order, and that day counts as day one.
scenes.shown: Where does the clock start? It does not start at the FIR date. It starts at the first remand order, and that day counts as day one.

scenes.dialogue: That is the Supreme Court's counting rule. And moving from police custody to judicial custody does not restart the clock.
These sixty or ninety days concern detention during investigation. The trial need not end within them. Prolonged undertrial detention has separate rules.
scenes.shown: These 60 or 90 days concern detention during investigation. The trial need not end within them. Prolonged undertrial detention has separate rules.

scenes.dialogue: Count with me. Ravi's case is in the sixty day category, with no special law extension. His first remand is on the first of January, twenty twenty six.
scenes.shown: Count with me. Ravi's case is in the 60-day category, with no special law extension. His first remand is on 1 January 2026.

scenes.dialogue: Mark that as day one. January accounts for thirty one days. February adds twenty eight, taking the count to fifty nine.
scenes.shown: Mark that as day one. January accounts for 31 days. February adds 28, taking the count to 59.

scenes.dialogue: The first of March is day sixty. No police report filed by then? The right arises on the second of March, day sixty one.
scenes.shown: 1 March is day 60. No police report filed by then? The right arises on 2 March, day 61.

scenes.dialogue: Ravi can then claim default bail and offer to furnish bail. But he does not simply walk out: he needs a court order and compliance with the release requirements.
Timing matters. Who moves first, your claim or the charge sheet? Suppose Ravi claims default bail as soon as the period expires.
Right then, no charge sheet has been filed, and he offers to furnish bail. A later charge sheet cannot defeat his claim, just because the court has not decided it yet.
But if a valid charge sheet is filed before he claims the right, default bail is ordinarily unavailable. He may still seek regular bail.
Be very clear: default bail rests on the missed statutory deadline. It is not an acquittal, and the investigation may continue after release.
Three questions to remember. Already in custody? Consider regular bail. Reasonably fearing arrest? Consider anticipatory bail.
Investigation deadline expired without the required report? Examine default bail immediately. Know the stage, check the section, act in time!
